old: "content": "Use simple invitation forms such as ¿*Quieres* *venir*? and ¿Te *gustaría* *venir*? to invite someone. Positive responses can use *Sí*, *claro*, *Me gustaría* or *Sí*, *quiero* *ir*. Keep the invitation focused on the event, time or activity. In this lesson the main aim is making and accepting invitations naturally."
new: "content": "Use *¿Quieres* + infinitive? to invite someone: *¿Quieres venir a la fiesta?* You know *querer* and *poder* from Unit 10, so you can also ask *¿Puedes* + infinitive? to check that the person is free: *¿Puedes venir el sábado?* To accept, say *Sí, claro* and add *Quiero ir* or *Puedo ir*. Keep the invitation focused on the event, time or activity."
why: 08-01 teaches ¿Te gustaría…? (polite-softening, Unit 26) and its table is about ya/todavía no: rewrite with quieres/puedes
gustaría examples replaced

old: "content": "*Quieres* and *gustaría* are not interchangeable in tone: ¿*Quieres* *venir*? is direct and casual, while ¿Te *gustaría* *venir*? softens the invitation — reach for *gustaría* when you want to sound more polite or less pushy."
new: "content": "*¿Quieres venir?* asks whether the person wants to come; *¿Puedes venir?* asks whether they are free. Both are friendly invitations, and *Sí, claro* answers either one."
why: tip about gustaría replaced

old: "content": "Use *ya* with the *pretérito* *perfecto* to say that something has already happened or has already been done. *Ya* normally appears before the participle or after the auxiliary: *Ya he preparado la cena*. In invitation contexts, it can explain that you have already made plans or preparations."
new: "content": "You know *ya* with the *pretérito perfecto* from Unit 2: *Ya he preparado la cena*. Here you use it to answer an invitation: when you have already made plans or preparations, say so. *Ya* comes before *he* or *hemos*, and the participle follows."
why: presents ya + pretérito perfecto as new (Unit 2); and states a position ("before the participle or after the auxiliary") that its own example contradicts
example 2 shows the lesson's point (declining with ya)

old: "content": "Use *todavía no* with the *pretérito* *perfecto* to say that something has not happened or has not been done yet. *Todavía no* normally comes before the auxiliary: *Todavía no he preparado la comida*. It is useful when responding to an invitation and explaining that preparations are incomplete."
new: "content": "You know *todavía no* with the *pretérito perfecto* from Unit 2: *Todavía no he preparado la comida*. Here you use it to answer an invitation and say that your preparations are not finished. *Todavía no* comes before *he* or *hemos*."
why: presents todavía no + pretérito perfecto as new (Unit 2)

old: "content": "Use *ya* to say that a preparation has been completed and *todavía no* to say that it remains unfinished. Combine these forms with food, drinks, dishes and traditions. The *pretérito* *perfecto* makes the connection with the present clear: *Ya he preparado el plato, pero todavía no he comprado la bebida*."
new: "content": "You know *ya* and *todavía no* from Unit 2. Here you combine them with food, drinks, dishes and traditions to say what is ready and what is still missing: *Ya he preparado el plato, pero todavía no he comprado la bebida*."
why: presents ya / todavía no as new (Unit 2)

old: "content": "Combine invitations with *ya* and *todavía no* to talk about plans and preparations. Use *ya* for completed preparations and *todavía no* for unfinished ones. Respond to invitations by accepting, explaining what you have already done, or saying what you have not done yet."
new: "content": "Combine invitations with *ya* and *todavía no*, which you know from Unit 2, to talk about plans and preparations. Use *ya* for completed preparations and *todavía no* for unfinished ones. Respond to invitations by accepting, explaining what you have already done, or saying what you have not done yet."
